🐛 Describe the bug
PyTorch 2.4 deprecated the use of torch.cuda.amp.autocast in favor of torch.amp.autocast("cuda", ...), but this change has missed updating internal uses in PyTorch. For example in DP here:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/parallel/parallel_apply.py
    
    
        Lines 92 to 93
      in
      3710a79

               enabled=autocast_enabled 
        
    
  


import torch

model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 10).cuda()
model = torch.nn.DataParallel(model, device_ids=[0, 1])
output = model(torch.randn(20, 10).cuda())
Produces:
/home/adrian/.conda/envs/lightning/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/nn/parallel/parallel_apply.py:79: FutureWarning: `torch.cuda.amp.autocast(args...)` is deprecated. Please use `torch.amp.autocast('cuda', args...)` instead.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The PyTorch code base contains several uses of torch.load internally, but not all of them set weights_only, which in PyTorch 2.4 raises a FutureWarning. Since these are internal, the user would see the warning but have no way of acting on it. PyTorch should set weights_only in all of its internal uses.
Some examples (but there are more if you search the code base):

  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/checkpoint/format_utils.py
    
    
         Line 87
      in
      f44739c
    
  
  
    

        
          
           torch_state_dict = torch.load(self.checkpoint_id, map_location="cpu") 
        
    
  



  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/optim/zero_redundancy_optimizer.py
    
    
         Line 111
      in
      f44739c
    
  
  
    

        
          
           obj = torch.load(buffer, map_location=device) 
        
    
  


There was a PR recently that resolved one of these important cases:
#130242
These warnings will show up in PyTorch 2.4.
This surfaced in our test suite (PyTorch Lightning) since we have configured them to fail if FutureWarning is raised.
If desired, I can send a PR to fix this.
Versions

import torch
from torch.testing._internal.two_tensor import TwoTensor
torch.manual_seed(123)

class Log(torch.utils._python_dispatch.TorchDispatchMode):
    def __torch_dispatch__(self, func, types, args, kwargs=None):
        if TwoTensor in types:
            return NotImplemented
        res = func(*args, **kwargs)
        if func is torch.ops.aten.mul.Tensor:
            print(f"\n{func}(*{args}, **{kwargs})")
            print(res)
        return res

a = torch.tensor([1+1j], dtype=torch.complex64, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)
b = torch.randn((1,), dtype=torch.complex64, device="cuda")

with Log():
    a * b.conj()

a = TwoTensor(a, a.clone())
b = TwoTensor(b, b.clone())

with Log():
    a * b.conj()
Leads to:
aten.mul.Tensor(*(tensor([1.+1.j], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True), tensor([0.9469-0.1451j], device='cuda:0')), **{})
tensor([1.0920+0.8018j], device='cuda:0')

aten.mul.Tensor(*(tensor([1.+1.j], device='cuda:0', requires_grad=True), tensor([0.9469-0.1451j], device='cuda:0')), **{})
tensor([0.8018+1.0920j], device='cuda:0')

aten.mul.Tensor(*(tensor([1.+1.j], device='cuda:0', grad_fn=<CloneBackward0>), tensor([0.9469-0.1451j], device='cuda:0')), **{})
tensor([0.8018+1.0920j], device='cuda:0')

First result is with plain Tensor and the next two are the two mul computation after the TwoTensor.
As you can see the result of the mul within the two Tensor is the result with the second argument being conjugated. So the Conj bit has not been handled properly somehow.
The current workaround for the user is to force resolving the conj so that lazy conj handling cannot break things by adding the following to the logging mode above:
        if func is torch.ops.aten._conj.default:
            res = res.resolve_conj()

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Subclasses of torch.nn.Module require calling super().__init__() at the start of the __init__ method. Suppose I have a torch.nn.Module subclass called A, and I want to create a subclass B of A which inherits some methods from A but has a different __init__ method (which doesn't call A.__init__):
import torch

class A(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("A")

    def method(self):
        pass

class B(A):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("B")

A()
# >>> A
B()
# >>> A
# >>> B
I had to call super().__init__() in B.__init__ in order to catch torch.nn.Module.__init__, but this required calling A.__init__, which I didn't want to do.
Solution
A solution to this problem would be if __init__ in torch.nn.Module was renamed to something like _torch_module_init. That way, B.__init__ could call self._torch_module_init() instead of super().__init__(), which sets the appropriate torch.nn.Module attributes while avoiding A.__init__:
import torch

class A(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        self._torch_module_init()
        print("A")

    def method(self):
        pass

class B(A):
    def __init__(self):
        self._torch_module_init()
        print("B")

A()
# >>> A
B()
# >>> B
For backward compatibility, torch.nn.Module.__init__ could simply call torch.nn.Module._torch_module_init, so existing torch.nn.Module subclasses which call super().__init__() still work, but __init__ can still be flexibly overridden by subclasses.
Alternatives
An alternative solution would be if A places its initialisation code in a separate method called EG _A_init, which can then be overridden by B (while avoiding the initialisation code for A, which is what I wanted), but in practise (IE a more complex example than shown below) this requires more boilerplate and feels more clunky/less intuitive:
import torch

class A(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._A_init()

    def _A_init(self):
        print("A")

    def method(self):
        pass

class B(A):
    def _A_init(self):
        print("B")

A()
# >>> A
B()
# >>> B
Additional context
No response
cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki

🐛 Describe the bug
In models where we do some operation dependent on a state variable existing (e.g: layer norm'ing some activation state if size > 0) which then is followed by a cat operation. We see that torch.compile fuses this operation which results in RuntimeError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered when the model is run with a state with size == 0.
This code errors on PyTorch version:  2.4.0a0+f70bd71a48.nv24.06
but not on PyTorch version: 2.1.0a0+32f93b1
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class BasicStatefulModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=64):
        super().__init__()

        self.linear_1 = nn.Linear(dim, dim)
        self.linear_2 = nn.Linear(dim, dim)

    def forward(self, x, state):
        out = state[0]
        if state.shape[1] > 0:
            out = self.linear_1(state[0])
        return self.linear_2(torch.cat([out, x], dim=0))


def test_state_cache_compile():
    dim = 64
    state_size = 2
    window_size = 128
    nstates = 2

    model = torch.compile(BasicStatefulModel(dim).to("cuda"), options={"trace.enabled": True}, disable=False)
    state = torch.randn((nstates, 0, dim), device="cuda")
    for i in range(100):
        x = torch.randn((window_size, dim), device="cuda")
        x = model(x, state)

        if state.shape[1] == 0:
            state = torch.randn((nstates, state_size, dim), device="cuda")
        state[0] = x[-state_size:, :]



if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_state_cache_compile()

🐛 Describe the bug
Setting dtype without dtype= to reshape() using a tensor works even though the doc doesn't explain it and an int tensor is returned instead of a float tensor as shown below:
import torch

my_tensor = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]])

my_tensor.reshape((3, 2), torch.float32)
# tensor([[0, 1],
#         [2, 3],
#         [4, 5]])
In addition, setting dtype with dtype= to reshape() using a tensor gets the error as shown below:
import torch

my_tensor.reshape((3, 2), dtype=torch.float32) # Error

TypeError: reshape() got an unexpected keyword argument 'dtype'

See:

As of 3477ee3 XPU backend in pytorch is missing torch.xpu.mem_get_info(). This function is required to support auto dispatch modes to run large models such as LLAMA 3 on the systems with devices which don't have enough memory to fit in the model. See [1] and [2] for details. It's supported for CUDA: https://pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.cuda.mem_get_info.html#torch.cuda.mem_get_info.

I am not sure if this is a bug or not, but I am getting a lot of new warnings after I upgraded to latest PyTorch and Executorch baselines (2.5.0.dev20240618+cpu).  I am trying to understand if I am doing something wrong, or if these warnings are unexpected.
Below is a simple example to reproduce the warning. I've defined a custom op using the examples in torch.library documentation (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/library.html) as reference. The warning comes when I use torch.export with a module that uses custom ops.
import torch
import torch.library
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

# --- Define a custom Op using torch.library --- #
lib = torch.library.Library("example", "DEF")
lib.define("custom_op(Tensor x) -> Tensor")

def custom_op(x: torch.Tensor):
    return x

def custom_op_fake(x: torch.Tensor):
    return x

lib.impl("custom_op", custom_op, "CPU")  
torch.library.register_fake("example::custom_op", custom_op_fake)

# --- Create a Model with the custom Op ---

# 1 input with multiple (debug outputs).
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64, 32)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(32, 16)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        y_fc1 = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        y = F.relu(self.fc2(y_fc1))
        return torch.ops.example.custom_op(y)

if __name__ == "__main__":

    # generate a uniform distribution of data.
    n_mini_batches = 10
    x_in = torch.distributions.uniform.Uniform(-1, 1).sample([n_mini_batches, 8, 64])

    # PRIME 1xN (debug)
    X = (x_in[1,:],)

    # export the model.
    m_export = torch.export.export(MLP().eval(), X).module()
This prints the following warning -
/opt/conda/envs/executorch/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/_subclasses/functional_tensor.py:362: UserWarning: At pre-dispatch tracing, we will assume that any custom op that is marked with CompositeImplicitAutograd and functional are safe to not decompose. We found example.custom_op.default to be one such op.
  warnings.warn(

I am not clear on what this means (and what I am doing wrong) as I am not doing any training (just converting a nn.Module into its FX graph representatation) , and hence Autograd should not be relevant here. My goal is to simply use FX and op transformations to implement a inference deployment workflow (similar to what Executorch does).
How can I modify this example to make this warning go away? Appreciate any help!

🐛 Describe the bug
Summary: Device information, correlation IDs, and the bytes field are missing in torch.profiler.profile JSON dumps when this profiling class is used on AMD GPUs.
test_kineto.py contains a script that (i) creates a tensor on each GPU, (ii) performs an allreduce.SUM operation across all ranks, while (iii) using the Kineto profiler to capture all CPU and CUDA events and (iv) dump the trace to JSON. When you run this script on AMD GPUs, the JSON is missing some attributes and information that are available when running the same profiler on Nvidia GPUs.
I ran the test_kineto.py script on (a) two Nvidia A100 80GB GPUs, and (b) two Instinct MI210 GPUs; using Python 3.9.19 and PyTorch 2. The output JSON files I got from these runs are available here (AMD Instinct MI 210) and here (for Nvidia A100).
1. Missing bytes field
For example, this is what a gpu_memcpy operation in the Nvidia trace looks like:
  {
    "ph": "X", "cat": "gpu_memcpy", "name": "Memcpy HtoD (Pageable -> Device)", "pid": 0, "tid": 142,
    "ts": 1720537333824533, "dur": 1,
    "args": {
      "External id": 334,
      "device": 0, "context": 1,
      "stream": 142, "correlation": 334,
      "bytes": 8, "memory bandwidth (GB/s)": 0.005813953488372093
    }
  }
On AMD GPUs, a similar gpu_memcpy item in the JSON file looks like this:
  {
    "ph": "X", "cat": "gpu_memcpy", "name": "CopyHostToDevice", "pid": 2, "tid": 0,
    "ts": 1720537542569197, "dur": 32,
    "args": {
      "External id": 131
    }
  },
The bytes field is missing in the latter. The same problem exists for all gpu_memset operations as well.
2. Missing device information
The A100 Kineto trace contains a field deviceProperties - this is completely absent/missing from the AMD trace.
  "deviceProperties": [
  {
      "id": 0, "name": "NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe", "totalGlobalMem": 84989575168,
      "computeMajor": 8, "computeMinor": 0,
      "maxThreadsPerBlock": 1024, "maxThreadsPerMultiprocessor": 2048,

      "computeMajor": 8, "computeMinor": 0,
      "maxThreadsPerBlock": 1024, "maxThreadsPerMultiprocessor": 2048,
      "regsPerBlock": 65536, "regsPerMultiprocessor": 65536, "warpSize": 32,
      "sharedMemPerBlock": 49152, "sharedMemPerMultiprocessor": 167936,
      "numSms": 108, "sharedMemPerBlockOptin": 166912
    }
  ]
3. Correlation ID
Each entry in the JSON generated on Nvidia GPUs contains a correlation ID:
{
    "ph": "X", "cat": "cuda_runtime", "name": "cudaStreamWaitEvent", "pid": 2012624, "tid": 1142494784,
    "ts": 1720537333825191, "dur": 1,

    }

This correlation field is not present in any of the events in the AMD GPU dump. For example, the MLCommons/chakra repository uses the torch.profiler.profile class, and assumes that this correlation field is present in the JSON in multiple places (e.g. here)

🐛 Describe the bug
contextlib.contextmanager is skipped by default in dynamo. Recently, #129091 added support for more complex context managers in GenericContextWrappingVariable. The same could be adapted to support contextlib.contextmanager.
import torch
import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def g(x):
    try:
        yield x.sin()
    finally:
        pass

@torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
def fn(x):
    with g(x) as y:
        z = y + 1
    return z

x = torch.randn(2, 3)
fn(x)

# torch._dynamo.exc.Unsupported: 'skip function g in file /micromamba/envs/pytorch/lib/python3.11/contextlib.py'

🐛 Describe the bug
In TensorDict, we sometimes need to match two lists of values extracted from dicts. We need these two lists to be sorted the same way (according to the keys of the first dict for instance). The code looks like this:
                source = dict(zip(keys, vals))
                return [source[key] for key in sorting_keys]
However this fails with dynamo, even though it's a totally unsurprising piece of code:
  File "/Users/vmoens/venv/rl/lib/python3.11/site-packages/torch/_dynamo/symbolic_convert.py", line 2751, in inline_call_
    sub_locals, closure_cells = func.bind_args(parent, args, kwargs)
                                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/Users/vmoens/venv/rl/lib/python3.11/site-packages/torch/_dynamo/variables/functions.py", line 515, in bind_args
    assert getattr(cell, name, name) == name
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError: 

from user code:
   File "/Users/vmoens/Repos/rl/tensordict/test/test_compile.py", line 237, in locked_op
    td3 = td + td2
  File "/Users/vmoens/Repos/rl/tensordict/tensordict/base.py", line 6582, in __add__
    return self.add(other)
  File "/Users/vmoens/Repos/rl/tensordict/tensordict/base.py", line 7101, in add
    other_val = other._values_list(True, True, sorting_keys=keys)
  File "/Users/vmoens/Repos/rl/tensordict/tensordict/utils.py", line 1129, in newfun
    return fun(_self, *args, **kwargs)
  File "/Users/vmoens/Repos/rl/tensordict/tensordict/base.py", line 4774, in _values_list
    return [source[key] for key in sorting_keys]

Set TORCH_LOGS="+dynamo" and TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE=1 for more information

This works though:
                key_to_index = {key: i for i, key in enumerate(keys)}
                return [vals[key_to_index[key]] for key in sorting_keys]

nodes.bodyText:
In torch.distributed.nn.functional._Broadcast, the below lines check whether the src and the rank are the same:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/nn/functional.py
    
    
        Lines 241 to 242
      in
      dfd1d19
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if ctx.src != ctx.rank: 
        

        
          
               gx.zero_() 
        
    
  


However, the src here is global rank in the default process group WORLD (required by dist.broadcast), while the ctx.rank

  
    
      pytorch/torch/distributed/nn/functional.py
    
    
         Line 231
      in
      dfd1d19
    
  
  
    

        
          
           ctx.rank = dist.get_rank(group=group) 
        
    
  


is a local rank under the provided process group by the function argument.
Thus this line fails to check whether the rank is the src, which results in all gradient to be zero for subgroups.

🐛 Describe the bug
Internal xref: https://fb.workplace.com/groups/6829516587176185/permalink/7507212116073292/
As a performance optimization, we maintain a hint on SymNode and use it preferentially in evaluate_expr rather than recomputing a hint from scratch from the expression every time we need it. In some cases, we do end up computing a hint like quantity (e.g., via maybe_evaluate_static); when we do this, we assert that the computed value is equal to hint, and assert fail if it is not.
In https://fb.workplace.com/groups/6829516587176185/posts/7501336323327538/ we observe that we nondeterministically fail with
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/_meta_registrations.py", line 3698, in meta_alias
      return self.view(self.shape) 
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/_refs/__init__.py", line 4587, in view
      return _reshape_view_helper(a, *shape, allow_copy=False)
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/_refs/__init__.py", line 3675, in _reshape_view_helper
      if a.is_contiguous():
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/fx/experimental/sym_node.py", line 460, in guard_size_oblivious
      r = self.shape_env.evaluate_expr(
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/fx/experimental/recording.py", line 245, in wrapper
      return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/fx/experimental/symbolic_shapes.py", line 5136, in evaluate_expr
      return self._evaluate_expr(orig_expr, hint, fx_node, expect_rational, size_oblivious, forcing_spec=forcing_spec)
    File "/data/users/ezyang/fbsource/buck-out/v2/gen/fbcode/17f95ac06b22dbae/aps_models/ads/icvr/__icvr_launcher_live__/icvr_launcher_live#link-tree/torch/fx/experimental/symbolic_shapes.py", line 5218, in _evaluate_expr
      assert static_expr == hint, f"{static_expr} != {hint}"
  torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised: 
  AssertionError: True != False

I haven't been able to identify why this is nondeterministically failing (TORCH_LOGS=+dynamic,sym_node do not diverge, until the failure point). However, inspection of logs during failure suggest a conceptually mistake in the code that we can fix even without a repro.
In some situations, an expression with unbacked SymInts can have a hint associated with it. In this particular case, we have:
evaluate_expr(Ne(u15, 1), hint=False, expect_rational=True, size_oblivious=True, forcing_spec=False

For some reason, we think that u15 != 1 should be False. Logs seem insufficient to diagnose further.

A simple script to reproduce this.
import torch 
import numpy as np
import torch.nn as nn

class MinimalExample(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, ):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear1 = nn.Linear(100,32)
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.linear1(x)
        return torch.mean(x, dim=(-1,-2))

torch_model = MinimalExample()
batch_size=1
    
x = torch.randn(1, 3,100, 100, requires_grad=True)
torch_out = torch_model(x)

torch.onnx.export(torch_model,               # model being run
                  x,                         # model input (or a tuple for multiple inputs)
                  "minimalist.onnx",   # where to save the model (can be a file or file-like object)
                  export_params=True,        # store the trained parameter weights inside the model file
                  opset_version=18,          # the ONNX version to export the model to
                  do_constant_folding=False,  # whether to execute constant folding for optimization
                  input_names = ['input'],   # the model's input names
                  output_names = ['output'], # the model's output names
                  dynamic_axes={'input' : {0 : 'batch_size'},    # variable length axes
                                'output' : {0 : 'batch_size'}})

import onnx
onnx_model = onnx.load("minimalist.onnx")
onnx.checker.check_model(onnx_model)
import onnxruntime

ort_session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession("minimalist.onnx", providers=["CPUExecutionProvider",]
                                               )

def to_numpy(tensor):
    return tensor.detach().cpu().numpy() if tensor.requires_grad else tensor.cpu().numpy()

    # compute ONNX Runtime output prediction``
ort_inputs = {ort_session.get_inputs()[0].name: to_numpy(x)}
ort_outs = ort_session.run(None, ort_inputs)

try:
    np.testing.assert_allclose(to_numpy(torch_out), ort_outs[0], rtol=1e-03, atol=1e-05)
except:
    print(print(torch_out,"\n", ort_outs[0]))
print(f"Exported model has been tested with ONNXRuntime, and the result looks good on CPU!")

Against what the doc of randint(), low, high and size argument with 0D or more D tensors work as shown below:


low (int, optional) – Lowest integer to be drawn from the distribution. Default: 0.
high (int) – One above the highest integer to be drawn from the distribution.
size (tuple) – a tuple defining the shape of the output tensor.


torch.randint(low=torch.tensor(-5),
              high=torch.tensor([5]),
              size=(torch.tensor([[3]]),
              torch.tensor([[[2]]])))
# tensor([[-2, 3],
#         [-4, 4],
#         [2, 1]])
Versions
import torch

torch.__version__ # 2.3.0+cu121

🐛 Describe the bug
The issue need to be reproduced with at least two gpus.
This is a regression in 2.3. After #119421, the following code no longer works with nccl 2.12.10 (nccl 2.13 works)
torchrun --nproc-per-node=2 demo.py
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist


if __name__ == '__main__':
    dist.init_process_group("nccl", init_method='env://')

    # rank = dist.get_rank()
    # local_rank = rank % torch.cuda.device_count()
    # torch.set_default_device(f"cuda:{local_rank}")
    # torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)

    dist.barrier()

output:

[rank1]: ncclUnhandledCudaError: Call to CUDA function failed.

If change the code to explicit call torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank), it works again.
I looked around but didn't find a nccl support policy, since both 2.2 and 2.3 compile and work well with nccl 2.12, I assume it is not out of date.
This issue can be reproduced with 2.3.1 release and same nccl version, also 2.4 branch with #130419.
I'm not familiar with nccl,
@eqy @kwen2501 maybe you know more about what happens here?

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi, I was hoping to get help using Inductor to compile programs with discontiguous outputs. This may seem like an obscure use case but it's important for certain hardware accelerators.
Inductor seems to use the wrong strides when torch.empty_strided creates an output tensor. In the following program, I expect the output strides to be (16,1), as in eager mode. Instead, Inductor uses contiguous strides of (8,1):
import torch

device = torch.device("cuda")
full = torch.randn((16, 16)).to(device)
view = torch.as_strided(full, (16, 8), full.stride())

def foo(x):
    result = x + x
    result_strided = torch.empty_strided(x.size(), x.stride(), device=device)
    result_strided[:] = result
    return result_strided

eager_result = foo(view)

compiled_foo = torch.compile(foo, backend="inductor")
compiled_result = compiled_foo(view)

assert compiled_result.stride() == eager_result.stride()

The assertion fails:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/brister/test_padding_wrong_strides.py", line 18, in <module>
    assert compiled_result.stride() == eager_result.stride()
AssertionError

This can lead to a correctness issue, as calling torch.as_strided on the output causes Inductor to return an invalid tensor:
import torch

device = torch.device("cuda")
full = torch.randn((16, 16)).to(device)
view = torch.as_strided(full, (16, 8), full.stride())

def foo(x):
    result = x + x
    result_strided = torch.empty_strided(x.size(), x.stride(), device=device)
    result_strided[:] = result
    return torch.as_strided(result_strided, result_strided.size(), x.stride())

eager_result = foo(view)
print('\n\nEager result:')
print(eager_result)

compiled_foo = torch.compile(foo, backend="inductor")
compiled_result = compiled_foo(view)
print('\n\nCompiled result:')
print(compiled_result)

🐛 Describe the bug
When Metal validation is enabled for macOS by setting METAL_DEVICE_WRAPPER_TYPE=1, it crashes with the following output:
validateComputeFunctionArguments:1056: failed assertion `Compute Function(gather_kernel_1): missing buffer binding at index 2 for size[0].'
Abort trap: 6

It appears to be caused by -setBytes:length: being given a length parameter of 0, which metal considers as not having set the buffer binding for that variable. Metal validation is turned on by default when running a macOS app from Xcode, so this crash can occur for PyTorch runs from Xcode without the developer understanding that it's due to Metal validation.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The specification of ONNX IR (hhttps://github.com/onnx/onnx/blob/main/docs/IR.md#names-within-a-graph) states:

All names MUST adhere to C90 identifier syntax rules.

However, the default PyTorch->ONNX conversion results in entirely illegal names containing at least dots, slashes and similar characters.
Repro
Let's serialize a very simple model to ONNX:
import torch

class Linear(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_shape: int = 784):
        super().__init__()
        self.input_shape = input_shape
        self.fc = torch.nn.Linear(input_shape, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x.view(
            x.shape[0], self.input_shape
        )  # num samples is first dim. Then flatten the rest
        x = self.fc(x)
        return x

sample_input = {'x': torch.randn(10, 784, 1) }
input_names = ['x']
dynamic_axes = { 'x': [0] }
model = Linear()

torch.onnx.export(
    model,
    args=(sample_input,),
    f="/tmp/traced.onnx",
    training=torch.onnx.TrainingMode.TRAINING,
    do_constant_folding=False,
    input_names=input_names,
    dynamic_axes=dynamic_axes
)
This will produce a graph with identifiers which contain illegal names. We can inspect them as follows:
import onnx

print(onnx.load("/tmp/traced.onnx"))

There are numerous identifiers of input, initializer and others containing ., / and similar. Some examples:
    name: "fc.weight"
    name: "fc.bias"
    name: "/Shape"
    name: "/Constant"
    name: "/Gather"
    name: "/Constant_1"
    name: "/Unsqueeze"
    name: "/Unsqueeze_1"
    name: "/Concat"
    name: "/Reshape"
    name: "/fc/Gemm"

These are not legal according to C90 specification.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Current state of the art research frequently uses exponential moving average and approaches like it to smooth model weight updates during treaining. In pytorch, this functionality is not yet implemented as a separate module.
Alternatives
Currently, there is an EMA Handler in Ignite but it doesn't fit in well with traditional training loops.
There is also an existing pip library that essentially implements most of the functionality (ema-pytorch). The suggestion here would be to collaborate with the author to implement that feature directly into the main Pytorch library.
Additional context
No response
cc @albanD @mruberry @jbschlosser @walterddr @mikaylagawarecki

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
I'm working on a dataset consisting of .raw images that I've processed and converted into 16-bit TIFF images (uint16). However, I encountered a challenge when trying to convert these 16-bit TIFF images into tensors for further processing in PyTorch.
The problem arises because the standard PyTorch tensor creation functions (like torch.tensor()) do not natively support the uint16 data type. PyTorch typically supports tensor creation for common data types such as float32, int64, and uint8, but uint16 is not among the directly supported types.
For my research, it is crucial to maintain the uint16 data type of the input images because altering the data type (e.g., converting to float32 or uint8) could lead to loss of precision or information, which could adversely affect the outcomes of my experiments.
Alternatives
No response
Additional context
No response

I don't see any related MPS max reproducers quite this simple on the issue tracker, so figured this might help. Working on an M3 Max, Python 3.12 with torch 2.3.1, I saw the max discrepancy vs. CPU below. This came up while I was investigating array API conformance in SciPy. I wonder if other more complex neural network MPS issues like #122030 might ultimately reduce to problems similar to this given that argmax is also similarly affected and obviously heavily used.
I was initially thinking this behavior might be "ok" because of #116567 (comment), where it is clarified that NaN sort-order is unspecified in torch. However, the array API specifies a requirement for NaN propagation from max (https://data-apis.org/array-api/latest/API_specification/generated/array_api.max.html#max) and the cpu device is already conformant.
Running:
import torch 

print(torch.__version__)
for device_name in ["cpu", "mps"]:
    tensor = torch.tensor([1.0, float("nan"), 3.0], device=torch.device(device_name))
    max = torch.max(tensor)
    print(f"{device_name=}, {max=}")
Produces:
2.3.1
device_name='cpu', max=tensor(nan)
device_name='mps', max=tensor(3., device='mps:0')

🐛 Describe the bug
There seems to be a difference in what eager mode and compiled mode outputs for the code snippet that follows.
TL;DR the code is trying to take two tensors and map the elements of the first tensor to the indices of the second tensors where the values are equal or 0 if the element does not exist in the second tensor.
Below is a minimal repro for the issue:
import torch

@torch.compile
@torch._dynamo.config.patch(capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops=True)
def minimal_repro(
    tensor: torch.Tensor,
    mapping: torch.Tensor,
) -> torch.Tensor:
    xx, yy = torch.meshgrid(mapping, tensor, indexing="ij")
    indices = torch.argwhere(xx == yy)

    mapped_values = torch.zeros_like(tensor)
    mapped_values[indices[:, 1]] = indices[:, 0]

    return mapped_values

def test_minimal_repro() -> None:
    tensor = torch.tensor([1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7])
    mapping = torch.tensor([0, 3, 4, 5, 7])

    mapped_tensor = minimal_repro(tensor, mapping)
    torch.testing.assert_close(mapped_tensor, torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 3, 0, 4]))
The test_minimal_repro code works with
 @torch._dynamo.config.patch(capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops=True)
being commented out but fails when the annotation is enabled.
mapped_tensor has the following value tensor([0, 0, 4, 1, 3, 0])

Original post
Python 3.13 is coming out in the near future - RC1 is planned for July 30 (first point at which the ABI is stable and packages can start releasing wheels for 3.13), and the fina release is planned for 1 Oct 2024 (see PEP 719).
I see that work on supporting 3.13 has started (gh-121979, gh-130030; Cc @atalman), but I couldn't find a tracking issue for the current status of it, so I thought it'd be useful to have one. The other motivation to open an issue now: we're working on implementing support for free-threaded CPython (a.k.a. "no-GIL", PEP 703) and are interested to start work on a first package that depends on PyTorch. Support for the default CPython 3.13 is a pre-requisite for starting that work though.
Here is a hopefully useful breakdown in steps to support Python 3.13:

 PyTorch builds from source on 3.13 (done in #126033 )
 Nightly cp313 wheels available for all platforms (waiting until final cpython rc)
 torch.compile support for 3.13 (complete @williamwen42 )
 PyTorch builds from source with free-threaded CPython (blocked on dependency support + update in core, tracking PR #130689)
 cp313t (free-threaded) nightly wheels available (blocked on ft build and dependencies)

nodes.bodyText:
Inductor is allowed to reorder the strides of intermediate tensors. user-defined triton kernels have different semantics depending on the striding of their input tensors. Nothing is stopping inductor from reordering the strides of inputs to triton kernels, so this can lead to silent incorrectness:
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def add_kernel(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr,
    n_elements,
    BLOCK_SIZE: "tl.constexpr",
):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(in_ptr0 + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(in_ptr1 + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

x = torch.randn(2, 2, device="cuda")
other = torch.randn(2, 2, device="cuda")

def f(x, other):
    y = x.t().contiguous().t()
    z = y.sin().t()
    grid = (z.numel(),)
    out = torch.empty_like(other)
    add_kernel[grid](z, other, out, z.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE=16)
    return out

f_compile = torch.compile(f)

out = f(x, other)
out_compile = f_compile(x, other)
print(out)
print(out_compile)
assert torch.allclose(out_compile, out)

NB: we have a similar problem with custom operators that we're working on fixing (#124647). Maybe we can share some of the infra there.

🐛 Describe the bug
There seems to be an issue where cdist will segfault on M1 Max for certain input sizes only, and only if numpy is loaded first. For instance, this is sufficient to segfault on my system
import numpy as np
import torch

t = torch.randn(18, 7)
dist_matrix = torch.cdist(t, t) # <-- Segmentation fault here

But somehow, this doesn't, even though it is a larger tensor
import numpy as np
import torch

t = torch.randn(30, 7)
dist_matrix = torch.cdist(t, t) # <-- No segmentation fault

If I import torch before numpy, this problem goes away
import torch
import numpy as np

t = torch.randn(18, 7)
dist_matrix = torch.cdist(t, t) # <-- No segmentation fault

And if I set the number of threads lower, the chances of segfaulting are less. For 1 thread it never segfaults, for 10 it always does, and for 5 it seems to have a 50/50 chance:
import numpy as np
import torch

torch.set_num_threads(1)
t = torch.randn(18, 7)
dist_matrix = torch.cdist(t, t) # <-- No segmentation fault, usually

This is with numpy 1.26.4, which was the very last version released before 2.0.0. 2.0.0 was released about a month before this writing and I haven't upgraded to it yet. I'm not sure if anything would change with that.

import torch

my_tensor = torch.tensor([])

torch.amax(input=my_tensor) # Error

RuntimeError: amax(): Expected reduction dim to be specified for input.numel() == 0. Specify the reduction dim with the 'dim' argument.

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
vLLM is a high-throughput and memory-efficient inference and serving engine for LLMs. We would like to use torch.compile to accelerate LLM inference. This issue is to track the progress of the integration.
The first step is to make torch.compile work for a minimal example of vLLM:
from vllm import LLM

# Example prompts.
prompts = ["Hello, my name is", "The capital of France is"]
# Create an LLM with HF model name.
llm = LLM(model="facebook/opt-125m")
# Generate texts from the prompts.
outputs = llm.generate(prompts)
To use torch.compile, we need to add self.model = torch.compile(self.model) in this line: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/worker/model_runner.py#L253 .
Currently, when I run it on H100 (with vllm 0.5.1), I get the following error:
